questions.stem: What is a model in predicate logic?

options.text: A model is a specific interpretation of a logical formula.
A model consists of a domain and an interpretation function.
A model is a set of logical formulas.
A model is a proof of a logical formula.

questions.explanation: A model in predicate logic consists of a domain of discourse and an interpretation function that assigns meanings to the symbols in the language.

distractorRationale.a: This describes an interpretation, not a model.
distractorRationale.c: A model is not just a set of formulas; it includes a domain and interpretation.
distractorRationale.d: A model is not a proof; it is a context for evaluating formulas.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about the formula $\forall x (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$?

options.text: It is true only if $P(x)$ is true for all $x$.
It is true if $Q(x)$ is true whenever $P(x)$ is true.
It is true if $P(x)$ is false for some $x$.
It is true only if $Q(x)$ is true for all $x$.

questions.explanation: The formula $\forall x (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$ is true if for every element in the domain, whenever $P(x)$ is true, $Q(x)$ is also true.

distractorRationale.a: The truth of $P(x)$ for all $x$ is not required for the implication to hold.
distractorRationale.c: The implication can be true even if $P(x)$ is false for some $x$.
distractorRationale.d: The implication does not require $Q(x)$ to be true for all $x$, only when $P(x)$ is true.

questions.stem: Given a model with domain \{1, 2, 3, 4\} and a predicate $R(x)$ true for $x = 2$ and $x = 4$, how many elements satisfy $\exists x R(x)$? Provide your answer as a number.
questions.explanation: The existential quantifier $\exists x R(x)$ is satisfied if there is at least one element in the domain for which $R(x)$ is true. In this case, $R(x)$ is true for 2 and 4, so two elements satisfy the formula.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a formula being true in a model and a formula being valid.
markingGuide: A formula is true in a model if it holds under the specific interpretation of that model.
A formula is valid if it is true in every possible model.
Truth in a model is context-specific, while validity is universal.
questions.explanation: A formula's truth in a model depends on the specific domain and interpretation of that model. In contrast, a formula is valid if it holds in all possible interpretations and domains, making it universally true.

questions.stem: What does the interpretation function in a model do?

options.text: It assigns truth values to logical formulas.
It assigns meanings to non-logical symbols.
It determines the size of the domain.
It provides a proof for logical statements.

questions.explanation: The interpretation function in a model assigns meanings to the non-logical symbols, such as constants, predicates, and functions, within the language.

distractorRationale.a: The interpretation function assigns meanings, not truth values.
distractorRationale.c: The domain size is independent of the interpretation function.
distractorRationale.d: Interpretation does not involve proving statements.

questions.stem: In a model with domain \{a, b, c\}, if $P(a)$ and $P(b)$ are true, and $P(c)$ is false, how many elements satisfy $\forall x P(x)$? Provide your answer as a number.
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier $\forall x P(x)$ requires that $P(x)$ be true for all elements in the domain. Since $P(c)$ is false, the formula $\forall x P(x)$ is not satisfied by any elements.

markingGuide: Select a domain with at least one element.
Ensure $P(x)$ is false and $Q(x)$ is true for at least one element.

questions.explanation: To falsify $\forall x (P(x) \lor \neg Q(x))$, choose a domain such as \{a\} and set $P(a)$ = false and $Q(a)$ = true. This makes $P(a) \lor \neg Q(a)$ false, falsifying the formula.

questions.stem: Which of the following is necessary for a formula $\exists x (P(x) \land Q(x))$ to be true in a model?

options.text: At least one element satisfies $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$.
All elements satisfy $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$.
No elements satisfy $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$.
At least one element satisfies $P(x)$ or $Q(x)$.

questions.explanation: The formula $\exists x (P(x) \land Q(x))$ is true if there exists at least one element in the domain for which both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are true.

distractorRationale.b: The existential quantifier does not require all elements to satisfy the condition.
distractorRationale.c: If no elements satisfy the condition, the formula is false.
distractorRationale.d: The formula requires both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ to be true for at least one element.

questions.stem: In a model with domain \{1, 2, 3\}, $P(x)$ is true for $x = 1$, and $Q(x)$ is true for $x = 2$. Which of the following formulas is true?

options.text: $\forall x (P(x) \lor Q(x))$
$\exists x (P(x) \land Q(x))$
$\forall x (P(x) \rightarrow Q(x))$
$\exists x (P(x) \lor Q(x))$

questions.explanation: The formula $\exists x (P(x) \lor Q(x))$ is true because there is at least one element in the domain that satisfies $P(x) \lor Q(x)$. Specifically, $x = 1$ satisfies $P(x)$ and $x = 2$ satisfies $Q(x)$.

distractorRationale.c: The implication fails for $x = 1$ since $Q(1)$ is false.
distractorRationale.d: There exists at least one element (e.g., $x = 1$ or $x = 2$) that satisfies $P(x) \lor Q(x)$.
